t: When You Shouldn't Enforce A Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/11/18/when-you-shouldnt-enforce-a-consequence/
q: One of the core tenets of SCM is to hold your students accountable for every rule violation. You do what you say you’re going to do. You follow through on your promises.
It’s when a student calls out without permission in order to stop a classmate from interfering with their right to learn.
Now, if you were to follow your classroom management plan as written and hold this student accountable for calling out, you would very likely alienate them.
Bear in mind that this is a student who has fully bought into the culture of your classroom. They care about learning and represent what you’re trying to inspire in others.
However, it’s important that you don’t just leave it at that. When you get a chance, later in the day, briefly apologize to the student who felt they had to stand up for themselves.
You’re showing understanding and compassion, and at the same time, making a statement through your actions that you respect the difference between the literal rule and the true spirit of the rule.
It makes you more human, more like them. It proves that you’re not a dictator, a robot, or a narrow-minded stickler without common sense.
x: If the situation is missed, the teacher should still hold only the original disruptor accountable, not the student who reacted.
There is a narrow exception to strict consequence enforcement: when a student breaks a rule in order to protect their own right to learn from a disruptive classmate.
He argues that holding this student strictly accountable would alienate a role model who has bought into the classroom culture, sending the wrong message about fairness and favoritism.

A private, later apology to the student who spoke up reassures them that protecting the class is the teacher's job, not theirs.
Linsin frames this as an example of respecting the spirit of a rule over its letter, which paradoxically strengthens rather than undermines a teacher's consistency.

t: Why Avoidance Is A Terrible Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
q: It’s avoidance. It’s limiting the healthy freedoms of students in order to avoid the possibility that misbehavior could occur.

Not to be confused with the effective use of consequences, these broad reactions punish students unnecessarily and send the message that they don't have the capacity to improve or do things the right way.
The alternative is to teach students in detail what your expectations are. Model for them, show them, how to behave during every activity, transition, task, and routine throughout the school day.
When we systematically and arbitrarily remove people, things, situations, and ideas they don’t naturally handle well, or may not like or agree with, we do them a disservice.
So instead of trying to avoid misbehavior by limiting the very things that help your students grow into responsible adults, outlaw the actual misbehavior itself.
We teach them patience, kindness, understanding, appreciation, self-restraint, discipline, discernment, and the tools to handle themselves with grace and aplomb.
x: Avoidance strategies — separating students, banning materials or activities because of past misbehavior — punish the whole group and signal that students can't improve.

He gives examples such as separating students who don't get along or banning materials like clay because they were misused, arguing that these blanket restrictions punish students unnecessarily and strip them of chances…
The alternative is to teach expectations in detail, model behavior for every activity and transition, and hold students accountable through clear rules and consequences.
He frames this as essential to helping students develop self-control, responsibility, and the ability to work with people and situations they don't naturally handle well.
The goal should be to outlaw the actual misbehavior itself, not the freedoms and opportunities that make misbehavior possible.
In this pointed critique, Michael Linsin takes aim at a common but misguided response to misbehavior: broadly restricting student freedoms rather than addressing the underlying conduct itself.

t: How To Stay The Course With A Tough Class
q: The tougher the class, the easier it is to be inconsistent. The easier it is to give in and lose control.
You must be, as Winston Churchill once said, “a peg, hammered into the frozen ground, immovable.
There is no one else to safeguard your students from disruption, bullying, being made fun of, and the like but you.
Ironically, with this mindset, not only will you never lose your job, but you’ll be admired by your colleagues, beloved by your students, and left alone by your principal.
When your class is out of control and the students seem so disrespectful, callous, and unmotivated, what you're seeing isn't who they really are.
In fact, in time it will become not just an attitude or mentality you carry with you to school every day. But who you are.
x: Staying consistent with a tough class requires deliberate mental toughness, since resistance to following through is universal and never comes naturally.
